sections.b: Jubilees retells Joseph's years in Egypt (Jubilees 39-45) more briefly than Genesis and adds its own emphases. Joseph refuses Potiphar's wife because he remembers Abraham's written commands against adultery, read to him by Jacob (Jubilees 39:6). As ruler he is the model official: no pride, no favoritism, no bribes, and Egypt has "no satan and no evil" (Jubilees 40:8-9). His master Potiphar and his father-in-law the priest of Heliopolis are one man (Jubilees 40:10). Joseph tests his brothers to learn "whether they had peaceful thoughts toward one another," and makes himself known when he sees their hearts united (Jubilees 42:25; 43:14). The divining cup of Genesis 44:5 becomes a cup Joseph "takes delight in" (Jubilees 43:10).

uncommon: Jubilees identifies Joseph's master Potiphar with his father-in-law Potiphera, priest of On (Jubilees 40:10; 44:24).

sections.b: Jubilees retells Genesis 38 in a way that eases Judah's guilt. His Canaanite wife Bedsuel, not Judah, keeps Shelah from Tamar (Jubilees 41:7), and Judah's admission "because I never gave her to my son Shelah" (Genesis 38:26) is dropped. Then Judah recognizes his sin, mourns and pleads with the Lord, and the angels tell him in a dream that he is forgiven (Jubilees 41:23-25). His line survives because Er and Onan never consummated their marriages with Tamar (Jubilees 41:27). In Jubilees 42:18-19 and 43:11-13 Judah, not Reuben, wins Jacob's trust and pleads for Benjamin.

Jubilees gives Tamar an origin Genesis never mentions: she is "from the daughters of Aram" (Jubilees 41:1), a kinswoman of Abraham's family, not a Canaanite. Er hates her because he wants a Canaanite wife like his mother (Jubilees 41:2). After she bears Perez and Zerah she is never given to Shelah (Jubilees 41:20). Judah's verdict that she is more in the right stands (Jubilees 41:19), but Jubilees drops his reason.

Jubilees keeps the levirate duty of Genesis 38:8, "do a brother-in-law's duty for her" (Jubilees 41:4), and Onan's refusal (Jubilees 41:5). It blames the withholding of Shelah on Judah's Canaanite wife (Jubilees 41:7), and it finds in the unconsummated marriages the reason why Judah's line was not cut off (Jubilees 41:27).

Jubilees sets death by burning for several sexual sins: for a man who lies with his mother-in-law or daughter-in-law, and for the woman (Jubilees 41:25-26), following Abraham's command (Jubilees 20:4; 41:28). Leviticus sets burning for taking a woman and her mother (Leviticus 20:14) and for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9), and death without naming the means for lying with a daughter-in-law (Leviticus 20:12). Jubilees also says the death sentence for adultery was decreed in heaven before Joseph's day (Jubilees 39:6).

sections.b: Genesis does not tell of Judah repenting over Tamar. Jubilees does: he knows his deed was evil, mourns, pleads with the Lord, and does not repeat it, and the angels tell him in a dream that he is forgiven "because he turned away from his sin and from his ignorance" (Jubilees 41:24-25).

Jubilees dates Joseph's famine to years 2171-2177 from creation and gives it natural causes: no rain fell on the earth (Jubilees 42:1), and in Egypt the Nile watered only a few places by its banks until it flooded again in the eighth year (Jubilees 45:9-10). Many Egyptians had stored grain on Joseph's example and fed themselves the first year (Jubilees 42:13-14). Jacob keeps the harvest festival with old grain, because not a handful of seed grew in Canaan (Jubilees 44:4).

sections.h: Jacob keeps the feast at Beersheba (Jubilees 44)
sections.b: Jubilees dates Jacob's journey so that he keeps the harvest festival of first fruits at the Well of the Oath, Beersheba, in the middle of the third month, with old grain because of the famine (Jubilees 44:1-4). Charles 1902 takes it as the Feast of Weeks on the fifteenth of the third month. The next day the Lord appears and tells Jacob to go down to Egypt (Jubilees 44:5).

In Jubilees Jacob waits seven days at Beersheba for a vision before going to Egypt (Jubilees 44:3-6), blesses God when he sees Joseph and declares the Bethel vision true (Jubilees 45:3-4), and rejoices that all twelve sons are safe (Jubilees 45:5). He dies at a hundred and forty-seven, exactly three jubilees (Jubilees 45:13), is buried in the double cave at Hebron (Jubilees 45:15), and leaves his books and his fathers' books to Levi (Jubilees 45:16).

Jubilees' list of Jacob's family who went to Egypt (Jubilees 44:11-34) reaches seventy by counting Jacob himself, leaving out Er, Onan, Perez's sons, Asher's grandsons and Dinah, and giving Dan and Naphtali five sons each. Charles 1902 sets out the sum: 29 + 14 + 14 + 12 = 69, and Jacob makes 70. Genesis 46:26-27 counts sixty-six and then seventy; the Greek Genesis, Exodus 1:5 in Greek, and Acts 7:14 have seventy-five.

At his death Jacob gives "all his books, and the books of his fathers" to Levi, to keep and renew for his descendants "until this day" (Jubilees 45:16). The verse makes Levi's line the guardians of a written tradition that runs back through Noah (Jubilees 10:14) to Enoch (Jubilees 4:17-19). Charles 1902 inferred that the author of Jubilees was himself a descendant of Levi and probably a priest.

Jubilees pictures Egypt under Joseph as at peace, "well ordered," with "no satan and no evil" (Jubilees 40:9). It calls On by its Greek name Heliopolis (Jubilees 40:10; 44:24), explains the famine by the failure of the Nile flood (Jubilees 45:9-10), and keeps Joseph's rule of a fifth for Pharaoh "to this day" (Jubilees 45:12).

Jubilees buries Jacob "in the double cave in the land of Canaan, near Abraham his father," in the land of Hebron (Jubilees 45:15). "Double cave" is the Greek Genesis's rendering of Machpelah (Genesis 23:9). Stephen's speech in Acts 7:16 follows another tradition, burial at Shechem.

Jubilees closes its list of Jacob's seventy descendants by saying that Er and Onan, who died childless in Canaan, "were counted among the seventy nations" (Jubilees 44:34): seventy souls of Israel set against the seventy nations of the world. The line is not explained in the text.
